title: Attention is limited
hook: we can truly attend to only a little at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, the invisible gorilla: viewers so busy counting passes that a gorilla walked by unseen. Your line was what am I missing.

A kitchen at six in the evening. A pot is about to boil over. A child is telling a long story about recess. A phone buzzes on the counter, and the radio is reading the news. All four want the same thing at once, and somehow it seems possible to give it to all of them. Then the pot boils over, and the child says, you're not listening. Both are right. So how wide can the beam of attention be?
screen: `A POT, A CHILD, A PHONE, THE NEWS.` → `YOU'RE NOT LISTENING.` → `HOW WIDE IS THE BEAM?`

segments.voice: William James answered in The Principles of Psychology. Attention, he wrote, is "the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought." One, out of several. And notice the small word seem. The kitchen seems manageable, but the clear, vivid kind of attention takes one at a time. Then James names the price: attention "implies withdrawal from some things in order to deal effectively with others." Every yes is a quiet no. To truly hear the child, something has to drop away, even for a moment. Some psychologists since James describe attention as a limited capacity. On that view, simple, practiced things can go together, like walking and talking, but for anything that needs real thought, the mind moves between tasks rather than holding them all. That matters on an ordinary Tuesday. If attention is limited, it's something precious, closer to a gift than a utility. Where it goes is what a person is actually spending. The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh wrote about washing the dishes only to wash the dishes, not hurrying through them toward the next thing. That isn't a rule against busy kitchens. It's an honest admission of the limit James described: a little at a time is how a mind really works.
screen: `ONE OUT OF WHAT SEEM SEVERAL.` · `EVERY YES IS A QUIET NO.` · `A LIMITED CAPACITY.` · `WASH THE DISHES TO WASH THE DISHES.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing to attend to: the breath, one sound in the room, or something in your hand, a cup, a stone, a pen. Give it the clear, vivid kind of attention James described, its weight, its edges, its temperature, and when the rest of your life knocks, let it wait outside the door while you come back to the one.
Attention is limited. The mind holds one thing clearly at a time, and every yes to something is a quiet no to something else. Today's word.
Your line: a little at a time. Every yes is also a quiet no. Day twelve sixty-five, done.

howItsDone: Some contemplative teachers train single-pointed attention by asking students to do one ordinary task, like washing dishes or walking, with full attention; psychologists study the same limit by measuring how performance drops when people split attention.
